results.title: Aberrant legal behaviour in frontal-network neurodegeneration: impulsive litigation and financial decision-making

output.summary: Impulsive and aberrant legal behavior is a recognized but underappreciated manifestation of bvFTD, mediated by orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex dysfunction. Patients may initiate multiple simultaneous lawsuits, sign contracts without understanding consequences, or make financial decisions that expose them to significant legal liability. Key clinical implications: (1) formal litigation capacity assessment is indicated to protect the patient from legal and financial harm; (2) bvFTD patients may lack capacity for legal decisions despite appearing competent in brief clinical interactions; (3) legal protection (power of attorney, conservatorship) should be considered for patients with documented orbitofrontal dysfunction.

results.title: Cognitive reserve and frontal-network neurodegeneration: masking of behavioural syndrome on standard cognitive testing

output.summary: High premorbid IQ and cognitive reserve can mask bvFTD on standard cognitive screening (MoCA, MMSE). The orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex — damaged early in bvFTD — is NOT well-tested by standard structured cognitive assessments, which rely on language, attention, and episodic memory. Social cognition tests (Reading the Mind in the Eyes, Theory of Mind, Faux Pas) and ecological validity tasks (Iowa Gambling Task, Multiple Errands Task) reveal the orbitofrontal deficit that standard tests miss. In high-IQ individuals, the gap between standard test performance and real-world behavioral dysfunction is widest. Key clinical teaching: in a high-functioning individual with clear behavioral syndrome and professional deterioration, a near-normal MoCA should NOT be accepted as evidence against bvFTD — social cognition testing is required.

findings.finding: STANDARD TESTS: MoCA 25/30. WAIS-IV Verbal Comprehension Index: 126 (Superior). WAIS-IV Similarities (abstract reasoning): 13/13 — SUPERIOR. WAIS-IV Vocabulary: 98th percentile. Standard executive tests (Trails B, DKEFS): 20th-30th percentile — below expected for his estimated IQ of 126+ but not dramatically impaired. CONCLUSION FROM STANDARD TESTS ALONE: Would appear to be a high-functioning individual with mild executive impairment.

SOCIAL COGNITION (THE KEY DIAGNOSTIC TESTS): Reading the Mind in the Eyes: 12/36 (<1st percentile — SEVERELY IMPAIRED). Faux Pas Recognition Test: 1/10 (SEVERELY IMPAIRED). Theory of Mind (Strange Stories): severely impaired — cannot attribute false beliefs or intentions. Moral judgment tasks: profoundly utilitarian with absent emotional resonance. Interpersonal Reactivity Index (self-report): Perspective Taking subscale: 4/28 (<2nd percentile).

ECOLOGICAL VALIDITY: Iowa Gambling Task: severely impaired — cannot learn from negative feedback, perseverates on losing decks. Multiple Errands Task: severely impaired — makes same errors 8 times without self-correction.

output.impression: Marked dissociation between superior verbal intelligence (estimated IQ ~126) and severely impaired social cognition (<1st percentile on Reading the Mind in the Eyes and Faux Pas Recognition Test) and ecological validity (severely impaired Iowa Gambling Task). Abstract reasoning and verbal comprehension are within the superior range on standardized testing, while social cognition and real-world decision-making are severely impaired. The pattern of severe social-cognitive impairment with sparing of verbal abilities reflects selective dysfunction of anterior-medial frontal networks subserving social cognition

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Recognise ceiling effects: standard cognitive scores can appear 'near-normal' in high-IQ patients with significant frontal decline.
Use social-cognition testing, functional history, and biomarkers (FDG-PET, genetics) rather than relying on global cognitive scores.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) and document functional decline.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given the high risk of impulsivity and impaired judgment in FTD.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Offer genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing options if a pathogenic variant is identified or suspected.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

patient.history_present_illness: Professor D is a 56-year-old tenured philosophy professor who is referred to the cognitive neurology clinic by his university's occupational medicine department after the department chair initiated a forced sabbatical due to 'serious concerns about professional conduct and teaching quality.' His sister, who lives nearby, is the primary informant as he himself dismisses all concerns as 'institutional politics' and 'academic jealousy.' Over the past 24 months, she has observed a striking transformation in her brother, who was formerly known for his precise, incisive intellectual thinking and warm mentorship of students. Approximately 2 years ago, he began missing scheduled lectures without notification — on four consecutive occasions in one semester, students waited for an hour and he did not appear. When confronted, he could not explain the absences and appeared unconcerned. He sent a 47-page single-spaced document titled 'A Fundamental Ontological Challenge to the Administrative Structure of the University' to the entire faculty via email — 47 pages of largely repetitive content circling the same themes. He sent follow-up emails to the same distribution list 11 times over the following week. He began sexual harassment of two PhD students — comments that his colleagues described as completely out of character for a man with a 28-year record of exemplary mentorship. He filed four simultaneous lawsuits — against the university, a former PhD student, his building management company, and an airline — none of which appear legally well-founded. He has stopped reading academic literature, which had been his daily practice for 30 years. He spends 12-18 hours per day on internet searches, repeatedly searching the same terms. His diet has narrowed to three specific foods. The professor himself, when seen by the examiner, engages in a sophisticated philosophical discussion about the epistemological validity of neuropsychological testing and the ethical implications of psychiatric labeling — he is clearly articulate and highly intelligent. His MoCA of 25/30 is near-normal and could lead to the conclusion that there is no significant cognitive impairment. His preserved language and abstract reasoning ability, combined with his skill at deflecting and reframing, allow him to appear cognitively intact on standardized testing despite a behavioral course that is disrupting his professional and personal life.
